title: There’s an awful lot we don’t know about data centers
gist: Nobody — including journalists, think tanks, or the tech companies themselves — can reliably say how many data centers were built in 2025 versus 2026, because 'data center' is not a federal regulatory category, 'planned' is undefined, and developers treat build data as commercial trade secrets. The data center backlash is therefore being legislated on top of a badly broken evidence base.

themes.theme: The data gap on data centers

insights.claim: There is no reliable public answer to whether more data centers are being built in 2026 than in recent years, despite dozens of published pieces on the data center backlash.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Policy and equity narratives about a data center building boom rest on numbers nobody can verify; treat 'construction is accelerating/decelerating' claims as unsourced.
insights.quote: I could not find an answer to this seemingly basic question
insights.locator: I had an idea for a post about data centers

insights.claim: Pew and the Manhattan Institute publish flatly contradictory rankings of the top data center states: Manhattan shows Virginia with more than twice as many data centers as Texas, while Pew shows a much narrower Virginia lead.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: State-level data center exposure screens built on either dataset can be off by a factor of two; cross-check before sizing regional power or REIT exposure.

insights.claim: Part of the Pew/Manhattan discrepancy is that they measure different units — Pew counts the number of data centers while the Manhattan Institute counts gigawatts of capacity — implying Texas facilities are smaller on average than Virginia's.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Facility counts and megawatt capacity are not interchangeable metrics; power demand forecasts should key off capacity, not site counts.
insights.locator: Pew and Manhattan are also counting different things

insights.claim: The word 'planned' is doing enormous unmeasured work: the Manhattan Institute uses a much more generous definition of a planned project, and many proposals exist in only vague form.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Announced-pipeline figures likely embed large speculative inventory; discount headline 'planned capacity' when modeling utility load growth.

insights.claim: A 'data center' is not a regulatory category as far as the federal government is concerned, so whether a campus counts as one facility or several is essentially arbitrary.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Any regulation or tax keyed to a per-data-center threshold is gameable by re-drawing site boundaries; expect developers to split or merge filings.

insights.claim: NTT Global Data Centers Americas operates VA-1 and VA-2 in Loudoun County as two distinct 'data centers' separated only by a Greek restaurant and a concrete-coatings business, while the Amazon/Anthropic campus in New Carlisle, Indiana is several buildings some of which are farther apart yet counted as one.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Illustrates why facility-count datasets are noise; anchor on gigawatts and capex, not building tallies.

insights.claim: Data on the pace of data center construction is partly withheld as commercial trade secret: a person working on data center deals at a major tech company said their team is only approximately aware of competitors' activity and actively works to obscure its own.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Competitive secrecy means third-party build trackers will structurally lag; sell-side capacity models are estimates of estimates.

insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Even the single most important cloud region cannot be mapped precisely — concentration-risk analysis of US-East-1 is inherently approximate.

insights.claim: Many new laws aimed at curtailing data center development are being written even though the underlying build-rate question is unresolved, so the issue has reached the public agenda in an undigested state.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Regulatory risk to data center development is rising on sentiment rather than evidence — a source of policy volatility for power and siting-dependent assets.
